conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’m so glad we have a chance to sit down together today. I know these first weeks with a new baby can feel like a whirl-wind of emotion and exhaustion, and I’m here to help you make sense of how you’re doing emotionally.

To do that, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s a 10-question tool designed to screen for symptoms of depression and anxiety that sometimes appear in the postpartum period. It also gently checks on thoughts of self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe and supported.

Everything you share is confidential, except in the very rare event that safety is a concern—then we’d talk together about next steps. There are no right or wrong answers; we simply want the most honest picture of how you’ve felt over the past seven days. We’ll go through each question one at a time, and you can answer in your own words. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

Let’s start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you used to—like small pleasures, a favorite show, a cup of tea, time with people you care about—or has that enjoyment slipped away?

I’ve still been able to enjoy things, actually. Yesterday I managed to finish an episode of the baking show I like, and I even laughed out loud at one of the contestants. It wasn’t quite the same carefree feeling I had before the baby—my mind still flits to whether she’s breathing in her crib—but the pleasure is definitely still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I’ve still been laughing—maybe not quite as loudly or easily as before, but when my partner sent me that silly meme about diaper explosions, I caught myself giggling. It feels good when it happens, just a little muted.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do find myself looking forward to little things—like tomorrow morning’s coffee or the short walk to the corner café with the stroller. The excitement isn’t huge, but it’s still there, kind of like a gentle “can’t wait” rather than the big buzz I used to feel.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if I put her diaper on crooked and we get a leak, I’ll think “oops, my bad,” but I don’t keep replaying it in my head or decide I’m a terrible mom. I just change her outfit and move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if her breathing sounds different, even though she’s perfectly fine—like last night I crept in twice to check on her. It’s not constant, and I can usually settle myself pretty quickly, but those little “what-if” moments do pop up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had that panicky, heart-racing kind of feeling. I do get a quick jolt of worry now and then—like when I hear a random noise on the baby monitor—but it passes as soon as I see she’s okay. Nothing that feels like real fear.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I keep things under control, but yesterday the sink piled up with bottles and she wouldn’t settle, and for a minute I felt like “ugh, how am I going to juggle all this?” It passed once she finally napped and I could finish the dishes.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s actually been one of the better parts—once I finally lie down, I’m out pretty quickly. I’m tired, but it’s that normal new-mom tired, not an “I’m too upset to sleep” thing.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had a couple of teary moments—like when I couldn’t get her to latch right away—but they’re short and I wouldn’t call myself sad overall. I feel pretty steady most of the time, just occasionally overwhelmed rather than down.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I really haven’t cried much at all this week—maybe one quick tear-up when a lullaby came on that my mom used to sing, but it was over in seconds and I felt fine right after.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind—not once. I want to be here for her, and I’ve never felt anything like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 8: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary  

Identified symptoms / concerns  
- Mild anhedonia: laughter and anticipatory enjoyment present but “muted” (Q1, Q2)  
- Transient, situation-specific worries about infant safety; no frank panic (Q4, Q5)  
- Occasional feeling of being overwhelmed when tasks accumulate; rapid resolution (Q6)  
- Brief, self-limited tearfulness; no sustained low mood or frequent crying (Q8, Q9)  
- No excessive guilt, self-blame, sleep-onset problems, or self-harm ideation (Q3, Q7, Q10)  

Pattern  
Overall emotional state is stable with situational, short-lived distress rather than pervasive depressive or anxiety symptoms.  

Screening significance  
Current presentation does not meet threshold indicators for major postpartum depression or generalized anxiety; no safety concerns identified. Continue routine postpartum monitoring and re-screen if symptoms intensify, persist beyond two weeks, or impair functioning.
